title: Ehud, left-handed (Judges 3:12–30)
hook: a left-handed man hides his sword where no one checks

segments.voice: Yesterday, the shofet, and the dial of Judges: stray, suffer, cry out, rescue. Your line was the cycle repeats. Today, the dial turns, and a rescuer arrives.

A short blade, two-edged, about a cubit long. A man straps it to his right thigh, under his clothes, and walks toward the palace of a king. He's carrying tribute, the payment his people owe to Moab. Nobody stops him. A man bringing gifts to a king is easy to wave through. The book has already told us the one thing about him that matters here: "Ehud the son of Gera, a Benjamite, a man lefthanded."
screen: `A TWO-EDGED BLADE, A CUBIT LONG.` → `STRAPPED TO THE RIGHT THIGH.` → `A MAN LEFTHANDED.`

segments.voice: The dial turns exactly as promised. Israel does evil again. Eglon, king of Moab, takes the city of palm trees, and Israel serves him for eighteen years. They cry out, and the Lord raises up a deliverer. His introduction isn't his strength, his family's fame or his faith. It's his left hand. The text doesn't explain why that matters. Some readers suggest guards would check a fighter's left side, where a right-handed man wears his sword; the story only tells us where Ehud hid his. Then it slows down. Ehud delivers the tribute and leaves with the men who carried it. At the carved stones near Gilgal he sends them on, turns back alone, and tells the king: I have a secret word for you. The king sends everyone out. Alone in the king's private upper room, Ehud says: I have a message from God for you. The king rises from his seat, and with his left hand Ehud draws the blade. The text tells the rest plainly and briefly: the king falls, Ehud locks the doors and slips out, and the servants wait outside, embarrassed, assuming the king needs privacy, until it's far too late. By then Ehud is in the hill country of Ephraim, blowing the shofar. Follow me, he calls, and the people take the fords of the Jordan, and the land has rest. A man introduced by one overlooked detail goes where no one thinks to look. The thing that set him apart is the very thing that let him through.
screen: `THE DIAL TURNS: MOAB RULES.` · `THE DELIVERER'S DETAIL: LEFT-HANDED.` · `A SECRET WORD, A MESSAGE FROM GOD.` · then, large: `WHERE NO ONE THINKS TO LOOK.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one thing about you that people tend to miss or count against you: being quiet, young or new, an accent, a different way of seeing, a skill nobody asks about. Hold it a moment without apologizing for it. Then ask where it could be exactly what's needed, one room, one problem, one person, and let a picture come.
Ehud. Son of Gera, of Benjamin, a man lefthanded: the judge raised up when Israel cried out, who carried a blade where no one checked and blew the shofar on the hills of Ephraim. Today's word.
Your line: left-handed. The overlooked detail was the whole story. Day seven hundred eleven, done.

chat.says: Why does the Bible bother telling us Ehud was left-handed?
options: The overlooked detail is the point: it's how the hidden blade got through.
It marks him as a priest, since priests carried the people's tribute.
It's only a family note; it plays no part in the story itself.
chat.meaning: The text introduces Ehud by his left hand, and the blade on his right thigh goes where no one thinks to look.

notes: Auditor: 'a cubit' renders gomed (3:16), a word found only here; its exact length is uncertain. The KJV and JPS 1917 both say 'a cubit', so kept.
Judges 3:15 is quoted from the KJV; please check JPS 1917 and switch if it matches.
'Eighteen years' is in Judges 3:14. 'A cubit' is in 3:16.
'The carved stones near Gilgal' renders pesilim (3:19), which the KJV gives as 'quarries' and other translations as 'idols' or 'graven images'.

The guard-checking explanation is offered only as 'some readers suggest'; the Hebrew phrase for left-handed (itter yad-yemino) and the Benjamin 'son of the right hand' wordplay are deliberately left out under the etymology rule.
The killing is told briefly and without gore by design; the 'covering his feet' euphemism (3:24) is rendered as 'the king needs privacy'.
